summary.title: How I wrote my own "proper" programming language
summary.one_liner: Learn why and how to design a real Java-style concurrent object-oriented language, using the Bolt compiler (OCaml frontend, C++ backend targeting LLVM IR) as a worked example.
keywords: protobuf serialisation between ocaml and c++
takeaways: Compilers work in stages: lexing, parsing, type-checking, desugaring/lowering, then code generation to machine instructions.
Targeting LLVM IR lets a language reuse LLVM's optimisations and multiple machine architecture backends.
Type systems can prove stronger properties than basic type checks, such as memory safety and data-race freedom.
Building your own language sharpens language design thinking, making it easier to learn new languages.
The Bolt series covers objects, inheritance, generics, concurrency and a second type-checking pass for data races.
summary.summary: This is the first post in a series by Mukul Rathi on building Bolt, a Java-style concurrent object-oriented language, rather than a toy language. It explains the motivation for designing your own language, then uses a telegraph-operator analogy to walk through compiler stages (lexing, parsing, type-checking, desugaring, and code generation), interpreted versus ahead-of-time compilation, and LLVM IR as an intermediate representation. It also introduces type checking and Bolt's two type-checking phases for traditional types and capabilities that prevent data races. The post is conceptual and previews the series, with the practical project setup deferred to part 2.
